entries.1087cb3b178283cd14c2983e9e2e7e474a7e8ba2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12468"/><div sID="gen22912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12468"/><hi type="bold">14. leave ... a meat offering and a drink offering--</hi>that is, give plentiful harvests, out of the first-fruits of which we may offer the meat and drink offering, now "cut off" through the famine (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.9">Joe 1:9</reference>, 13, 16). "Leave behind Him": as God in visiting His people now has left behind Him a curse, so He will, on returning to visit them, leave behind Him a blessing. <div eID="gen22912" type="x-p"/>
entries.7506c04cf43615c23208bcaee7886d8fce72daaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12469"/><div sID="gen22913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12469"/><hi type="bold">15. Blow the trumpet--</hi>to convene the people (<reference osisRef="Num.10.3">Nu 10:3</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>. The nation was guilty, and therefore there must be a national humiliation. Compare Hezekiah's proceedings before Sennacherib's invasion (<reference osisRef="2Chr.30.1-2Chr.30.27">2Ch 30:1-27</reference>). <div eID="gen22913" type="x-p"/>
entries.c673178f3f4dcc85e7f5fd3aa81b3bc3970ffc02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12470"/><div sID="gen22914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12470"/><hi type="bold">16. sanctify the congregation--</hi>namely, by expiatory rites and purification with water [Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.10">Ex 19:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.22">22</reference>). Maurer translates, "appoint a solemn assembly," which would be a tautological repetition of <reference osisRef="Joel.2.15">Joe 2:15</reference>.<div eID="gen22914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">elders ... children--</hi>No age was to be excepted (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.13">2Ch 20:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bridegroom--</hi>ordinarily exempted from public duties (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.5">De 24:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">1Co 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.29">29</reference>).<div eID="gen22916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">closet--</hi>or, nuptial bed, from a Hebrew root "to cover," referring to the canopy over it. <div eID="gen22917" type="x-p"/>
entries.a56d03894867cfe62a86a81eabed11bdd79e187a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12471"/><div sID="gen22918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12471"/><hi type="bold">17. between the porch and ... altar--</hi>the porch of Solomon's temple on the east (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.3">1Ki 6:3</reference>); the altar of burnt offerings in the court of the priests, before the porch (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12">2Ch 8:12</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Mt 23:35</reference>). The suppliants thus were to stand with their backs to the altar on which they had nothing to offer, their faces towards the place of the Shekinah presence.<div eID="gen22918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heathen should rule over them--</hi>This shows that not locusts, but human foes, are intended. The Margin translation, "use a byword against them," is not supported by the Hebrew.<div eID="gen22919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherefore should they say ... Where is their God?--</hi>that is, do not for thine own honor's sake, let the heathen sneer at the God of Israel, as unable to save His people (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">Psa 79:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">115:2</reference>). <div eID="gen22920" type="x-p"/>
entries.e90cbdc562827179d953802fe42958173587853c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12472"/><div sID="gen22921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12472"/><hi type="bold">18. Then--</hi>when God sees His people penitent.<div eID="gen22921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be jealous for his land--</hi>as a husband jealous of any dishonor done to the wife whom he loves, as if done to himself. The Hebrew comes from an Arabic root, "to be flushed in face" through indignation. <div eID="gen22922" type="x-p"/>
entries.7642720d456bce07c68e19bae966b3efba70a4df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12473"/><div sID="gen22923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12473"/><hi type="bold">19. corn ... wine ... oil--</hi>rather, as Hebrew, "the corn ... the wine ... the oil," namely, which the locusts have destroyed [Henderson]. Maurer not so well explains, "the corn, &c., necessary for your sustenance." "The Lord will answer," namely, the prayers of His people, priests, and prophets. Compare in the case of Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.20">2Ki 19:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">21</reference>. <div eID="gen22923" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee7bd706ad60a94146a37c78b332173fdf45ba57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12474"/><div sID="gen22924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12474"/><hi type="bold">20. the northern army--</hi>The Hebrew expresses that the north in relation to Palestine is not merely the quarter whence the invader comes, but is his native land, "the Northlander"; namely, the Assyrian or Babylonian (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.1.14">Jr 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.13">Zep 2:13</reference>). The locust's native country is not the north, but the south, the deserts of Arabia, Egypt, and Libya. Assyria and Babylon are the type and forerunner of all Israel's foes (Rome, and the final Antichrist), from whom God will at last deliver His people, as He did from Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>).<div eID="gen22924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">face ... hinder part--</hi>more applicable to a human army's van and rear, than to locusts. The northern invaders are to be dispersed in every other direction but that from which they had come: "a land barren and desolate," that is, Arabia-Deserta: "the eastern (or front) sea," that is, the Dead Sea: "the utmost (or hinder) sea," that is, the Mediterranean. In front and behind mean east and west; as, in marking the quarters of the world, they faced the east, which was therefore "in front"; the west was behind them; the south was on their right, and the north on their left.<div eID="gen22925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stink--</hi>metaphor from locusts, which perish when blown by a storm into the sea or the desert, and emit from their putrefying bodies such a stench as often breeds a pestilence.<div eID="gen22926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because he hath done great things--</hi>that is, because the invader hath haughtily magnified himself in his doings. Compare as to Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.11-2Kgs.13.22">2Ki 19:11-13, 22</reference>, 28. This is quite inapplicable to the locusts, who merely seek food, not self-glorification, in invading a country. <div eID="gen22927" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f1a56e442a2a92c1d2c1e5d0b6fc0c51a9aeca1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12475"/><div sID="gen22928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12475"/>21-23. In an ascending gradation, the land destroyed by the enemy, the beasts of the field, and the children of Zion, the land's inhabitants, are addressed, the former two by personification.<div eID="gen22928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord will do great things--</hi>In contrast to the "great things" done by the haughty foe (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.20">Joe 2:20</reference>) to the hurt of Judah stand the "great things" to be done by Jehovah for her benefit (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.126.2">Psa 126:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.3">3</reference>). <div eID="gen22929" type="x-p"/>
entries.30855b98643f044fd53c67ab2a1919fe760e9ac6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12478"/><div sID="gen22934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12478"/>24. The effect of the seasonable rains shall be abundance of all articles of food. <div eID="gen22934" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdeb353b0d21c205f19562619f67406e5c79f5b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12479"/><div sID="gen22935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12479"/><hi type="bold">25. locust ... cankerworm ... caterpiller ... palmer worm--</hi>the reverse order from <reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">Joe 1:4</reference>, where (see on <reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">Joe 1:4</reference>) God will restore not only what has been lost by the full-grown consuming locust, but also what has been lost by the less destructive licking locust, and swarming locust, and gnawing locust. <div eID="gen22935" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2a31c2db9ae839c0deecc6b120228027e388f2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12480"/><div sID="gen22936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12480"/><hi type="bold">26. never be ashamed--</hi>shall no longer endure the "reproach of the heathen (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joe 2:17</reference>), [Maurer]; or rather, "shall not bear the shame of disappointed hopes," as the husbandmen had heretofore (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.11">Joe 1:11</reference>). So spiritually, waiting on God, His people shall not have the shame of disappointment in their expectations from Him (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.33">Ro 9:33</reference>). <div eID="gen22936" type="x-p"/>
entries.7442ea4af7abd50a5d13585534ab89fb186e89a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12481"/><div sID="gen22937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12481"/><hi type="bold">27. know that I am in the midst of Israel--</hi>As in the Old Testament dispensation God was present by the Shekinah, so in the New Testament first, for a brief time by the Word made flesh dwelling among us (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>), and to the close of this dispensation by the Holy Spirit in the Church (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>), and probably in a more perceptible manner with Israel when restored (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.26-Ezek.37.28">Eze 37:26-28</reference>).<div eID="gen22937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">never be ashamed--</hi>not an unmeaning repetition from <reference osisRef="Joel.2.26">Joe 2:26</reference>. The twice-asserted truth enforces its unfailing certainty. As the "shame" in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.26">Joe 2:26</reference> refers to temporal blessings, so in this verse it refers to the spiritual blessings flowing from the presence of God with His people (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jr 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>). <div eID="gen22938" type="x-p"/>
entries.518cf9d0ff354078ab2959b659ec6998d6dc7102: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12482"/><div sID="gen22939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12482"/><hi type="bold">28. afterward--</hi>"in the last days" (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>) under Messiah after the invasion and deliverance of Israel from the northern army. Having heretofore stated the outward blessings, he now raises their minds to the expectation of extraordinary spiritual blessings, which constitute the true restoration of God's people (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Is 44:3</reference>). Fulfilled in earnest (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.17">Ac 2:17</reference>) on Pentecost; among the Jews and the subsequent election of a people among the Gentiles; hereafter more fully at the restoration of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Is 54:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.9">Jr 31:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.29">Eze 39:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>) and the consequent conversion of the whole world (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">11:9</reference>; 66:18-23; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Ro 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">15</reference>). As the Jews have been the seedmen of the elect Church gathered out of Jews and Gentiles, the first Gospel preachers being Jews from Jerusalem, so they shall be the harvest men of the coming world-wide Church, to be set up at Messiah's appearing. That the promise is not restricted to the first Pentecost appears from Peter's own words: "The promise is (not only) unto you and to your children, (but also) to all that are afar off (both in space and in time), even as many as the Lord our God shall call" (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Ac 2:39</reference>). So here "upon all flesh."<div eID="gen22939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will pour out--</hi>under the new covenant: not merely, let fall drops, as under the Old Testament (<reference osisRef="John.7.39">Joh 7:39</reference>).<div eID="gen22940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my spirit--</hi>the Spirit "proceeding from the Father and the Son," and at the same time one with the Father and the Son (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Is 11:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sons ... daughters ... old ... young--</hi>not merely on a privileged few (<reference osisRef="Num.11.29">Nu 11:29</reference>) as the prophets of the Old Testament, but men of all ages and ranks. See <reference osisRef="Acts.21.9">Ac 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.5">1Co 11:5</reference>, as to "daughters," that is, women, prophesying.<div eID="gen22942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dreams ... visions--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.9.10">Ac 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.9">16:9</reference>). The "dreams" are attributed to the "old men," as more in accordance with their years; "visions" to the "young men," as adapted to their more lively minds. The three modes whereby God revealed His will under the Old Testament (<reference osisRef="Num.12.6">Nu 12:6</reference>), "prophecy, dreams, and visions," are here made the symbol of the full manifestation of Himself to all His people, not only in miraculous gifts to some, but by His indwelling Spirit to all in the New Testament (<reference osisRef="John.14.21">Joh 14:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">15:15</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Acts.16.9">Ac 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.9">18:9</reference>, the term used is "vision," though in the night, not a dream. No other dream is mentioned in the New Testament save those given to Joseph in the very beginning of the New Testament, before the full Gospel had come; and to the wife of Pilate, a Gentile (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.20">Mt 1:20</reference>; 2:13; 27:19). "Prophesying" in the New Testament is applied to all speaking under the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, and not merely to foretelling events. All true Christians are "priests" and "ministers" of our God (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">Is 61:6</reference>), and have the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.26">Eze 36:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.27">27</reference>). Besides this, probably, a special gift of prophecy and miracle-working is to be given at or before Messiah's coming again. <div eID="gen22943" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb656931ba6276fb58d8a9ca8251e7bc47039b20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12483"/><div sID="gen22944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12483"/><hi type="bold">29. And also--</hi>"And even." The very slaves by becoming the Lord's servants are His freemen (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col 3:11</reference>; Phm 16). Therefore, in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.18">Ac 2:18</reference> it is quoted, "My servants" and "My handmaidens"; as it is only by becoming the Lord's servants they are spiritually free, and partake of the same spirit as the other members of the Church. <div eID="gen22944" type="x-p"/>
entries.ded0e27705eae5f68378937e7dd19a2b83ca26e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12484"/><div sID="gen22945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12484"/>30-31. As Messiah's manifestation is full of joy to believers, so it has an aspect of wrath to unbelievers, which is represented here. Thus when the Jews received Him not in His coming of grace, He came in judgment on Jerusalem. Physical prodigies, massacres, and conflagrations preceded its destruction [Josephus, Wars of the Jews]. To these the language here may allude; but the figures chiefly symbolize political revolutions and changes in the ruling powers of the world, prognosticated by previous disasters (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Am 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Mt 24:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.25-Luke.21.27">Lu 21:25-27</reference>), and convulsions such as preceded the overthrow of the Jewish polity. Such shall probably occur in a more appalling degree before the final destruction of the ungodly world ("the great and terrible day of Jehovah," compare Mal 4:5), of which Jerusalem's overthrow is the type and earnest. <div eID="gen22945" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bba6527a0fd41fbfa9521548a99d4fe30016b00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12485"/><div sID="gen22946" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12485"/><hi type="bold">32. call on ... name of ... Lord--</hi>Hebrew, Jehovah. Applied to Jesus in <reference osisRef="Rom.10.13">Ro 10:13</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.9.14">Ac 9:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.2">1Co 1:2</reference>). Therefore, Jesus is Jehovah; and the phrase means, "Call on Messiah in His divine attributes."<div eID="gen22946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be delivered--</hi>as the Christians were, just before Jerusalem's destruction, by retiring to Pella, warned by the Saviour (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">Mt 24:16</reference>); a type of the spiritual deliverance of all believers, and of the last deliverance of the elect "remnant" of Israel from the final assault of Antichrist. "In Zion and Jerusalem" the Saviour first appeared; and there again shall He appear as the Deliverer (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.1-Zech.14.5">Zec 14:1-5</reference>).<div eID="gen22947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the Lord hath said--</hi>Joel herein refers, not to the other prophets, but to his own words preceding.<div eID="gen22948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call--</hi>metaphor from an invitation to a feast, which is an act of gratuitous kindness (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.16">Lu 14:16</reference>). So the remnant called and saved is according to the election of grace, not for man's merits, power, or efforts (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Ro 11:5</reference>). <chapter eID="Joel.2"/>

entries.7cd3b3e5ef9e08df3ab90d9a0668bc15a92fa0a5: <div eID="gen34066" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34067" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34068" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34068" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34067" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34069" type="x-p"/> The prophet sounds the alarm of a dreadful calamity, the description of which is most terribly worked up, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.1-Joe.2.11">Joe 2:1-11</reference>. Exhortation to repentance, fasting, and prayer, that the Divine judgments may be averted, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.12-Joe.2.17">Joe 2:12-17</reference>. God will in due time take vengeance on all the enemies of pure and undefiled religion, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.18-Joe.2.20">Joe 2:18-20</reference>. Great prosperity of the Jews subsequent to their return from the Babylonish captivity, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.21-Joe.2.27">Joe 2:21-27</reference>. Joel then makes an elegant transition to the outpouring of the Holy Ghost on the day of Pentecost, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.28-Joe.2.30">Joe 2:28-30</reference>; for so these verses are explained by one of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. See <reference osisRef="Act.2.16-Act.2.21">Act 2:16-21</reference>. Prophecy concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, which was shortly to follow the opening of the Gospel dispensation, <reference osisRef="Act.2.31">Act 2:31</reference>. Promises of safety to the faithful and penitent; promises afterwards remarkably fulfilled to the Christians in their escape to Pella from the desolating sword of the Roman army, <reference osisRef="Act.2.32">Act 2:32</reference>. <div eID="gen34069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34070" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34071" type="x-p"/> Blow ye the trumpet in Zion - This verse also shows that the temple was still standing. All assemblies of the people were collected by the sound of the trumpet. <div eID="gen34071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34072" type="x-p"/> The day of the Lord cometh - This phrase generally means a day of judgment or punishment.
entries.41ab0a3e78261ba70dabb1c8a7d076900121173a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34073" type="x-p"/> A day of darkness, etc - The depredations of the locusts are described from the second to the eleventh verse, and their destruction in the twentieth. Dr. Shaw, who saw locusts in Barbary in 1724 and 1725, thus describes them: - "I never observed the mantes, bald locusts, to be gregarious. But the locusts, properly so called, which are so frequently mentioned by sacred as well as profane writers, are sometimes so beyond expression. Those which I saw in 1724 and 1725 were much bigger than our common grasshopper; and had brown spotted wings, with legs and bodies of a bright yellow. Their first appearance was toward the latter end of March, the wind having been for some time south. In the middle of April their numbers were so vastly increased that, in the heat of the day, they formed themselves into large and numerous swarms; flew in the air like a succession of clouds; and, as the prophet Joel expresses it, (<reference osisRef="Joe.2.10">Joe 2:10</reference>) they darkened the sun. When the wind blew briskly, so that these swarms were crowded by others, or thrown one upon another, we had a lively idea of that comparison of the psalmist, (<reference osisRef="Psa.109.23">Psa 109:23</reference>), of being 'tossed up and down as the locust.' In the month of May, when the ovaries of those insects were ripe and turgid, each of these swarms began gradually to disappear; and retired into the Mettijiah, and other adjacent plains, where they deposited their eggs. These were no sooner hatched in June, than each of these broods collected itself into a compact body of a furlong or more in square; and, marching immediately forward in the direction of the sea, they let nothing escape them; eating up every thing that was green and juicy, not only the lesser kinds of vegetables, but the vine likewise; the fig tree, the pomegranate, the palm, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, <reference osisRef="Joe.1.12">Joe 1:12</reference>; in doing which they kept their ranks like men of war; climbing over, as they advanced, every tree or wall that was in their way. Nay, they entered into our very houses and bedchambers, like so many thieves. The inhabitants, to stop their progress, made a variety of pits and trenches all over their fields and gardens, which they filled with water; or else they heaped up in them heath, stubble, and such like combustible matter, which were severally set on fire upon the approach of the locusts. But this was all to no purpose, for the trenches were quickly filled up, and the fires extinguished, by infinite swarms succeeding one another; while the front was regardless of danger, and the rear pressed on so close, that a retreat was altogether impossible. A day or two after one of these broods was in motion, others were already hatched to march and glean after them; gnawing off the very bark, and the young branches, of such trees as had before escaped with the loss only of their fruit and foliage. So justly have they been compared by the prophet Joel (<reference osisRef="Joe.2.3">Joe 2:3</reference>) to a great army; who further observes, that 'the land is as the garden of Eden before them and behind them a desolate wilderness.' "Having lived near a month in this manner (like a μυριοστομον ξιφος, or sword with ten thousand edges, to which they have been compared), upon the ruin and destruction of every vegetable substance which came in their way, they arrived at their full growth, and threw old their nympha state by casting their outward skin. To prepare themselves for this change, they clung by their hinder feet to some bush, twig, or corner of a stone; and immediately, by using an undulating motion, their heads would first break out, and then the rest of their bodies. The whole transformation was performed in seven or eight minutes, after which they lay for a short time in a torpid and seemingly languishing condition; but as soon ad the sun and air had hardened their wings, by drying up the moisture which remained upon them, after casting their sloughs, they reassumed their former voracity, with an addition both of strength and agility. Yet they did not continue long in this state before they were entirely dispersed, as their parents were before, after they had laid their eggs; and as the direction of the marches and flights of them both was always to the northward, and not having strength, as they have sometimes had, to reach the opposite shores of Italy France, or Spain, it is probable they perished in the sea, a grave which, according to these people, they have in common with other winged creatures." - Travels, 4to. edition pp. 187, 188. <div eID="gen34073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34074" type="x-p"/> A day of darkness - They sometimes obscure the sun. And Thuanus observes of an immense crowd, that "they darkened the sun at mid-day." <div eID="gen34074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34075" type="x-p"/> As the morning spread upon the mountains - They appeared suddenly: as the sun, in rising behind the mountains, shoots his rays over them. Adanson, in his voyage to Senegal, says: "Suddenly there came over our heads a thick cloud which darkened the air, and deprived us or the rays of the sun. We soon found that it was owing to a cloud of locusts." Some clouds of them are said to have darkened the sun for a mile, and others for the space of twelve miles! See the note on <reference osisRef="Joe.2.10">Joe 2:10</reference> (note).
entries.a912f6f5081bbdcb9969c6be830734b4c39a2514: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34076" type="x-p"/> A fire devoureth before them - They consume like a general conflagration. "They destroy the ground, not only for the time, but burn trees for two years after." Sir Hans Sloane, Nat. Hist. of Jamaica, vol. i., p. 29. <div eID="gen34076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34077" type="x-p"/> Behind them a flame burneth - "Wherever they feed," says Ludolf, in his History of Ethiopia, "their leavings seem as if parched with fire." <div eID="gen34077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34078" type="x-p"/> Nothing shall escape them - "After devouring the herbage," says Adanson, "with the fruits and leaves of trees, they attacked even the buds and the very bark; they did not so much as spare the reeds with which the huts were thatched."
entries.f7eae1a12dd74d3c9fbb8866730536a397a40a36: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34079" type="x-p"/> The appearance of horses - The head of the locust is remarkably like that of the horse; and so Ray on Insects describes them: Caput oblongum, equi instar, prona spectans - "They have an oblong head, like to that of a horse, bending downward." On this account the Italians call them cavaletta, cavalry. Bochart remarks, from an Arabic writer, that the locusts resemble ten different kinds of animals: <div eID="gen34079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34080" type="x-p"/> 1. The Horse in its head. <div eID="gen34080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34081" type="x-p"/> 2. The Elephant in its eyes. <div eID="gen34081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34082" type="x-p"/> 3. The Bull in its neck. <div eID="gen34082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34083" type="x-p"/> 4. The Stag in its horns. <div eID="gen34083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34084" type="x-p"/> 5. The Lion in its breast. <div eID="gen34084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34085" type="x-p"/> 6. The Scorpion in its belly. <div eID="gen34085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34086" type="x-p"/> 7. The Eagle in its wings. <div eID="gen34086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34087" type="x-p"/> 8. The Camel in its thighs. <div eID="gen34087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34088" type="x-p"/> 9. The Ostrich in its feet. And <div eID="gen34088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34089" type="x-p"/> 10. The Serpent in its tail. <div eID="gen34089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34090" type="x-p"/> Vid. Hieroz., vol. ii., p. 475, edit. 1692. <div eID="gen34090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34091" type="x-p"/> But its most prominent resemblance is to the horse, which the prophet mentions; and which the Arabic writer puts in the first place, as being the chief.
entries.3dd9d774bf4b5972173aa3d9d2d652a98f52b435: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34092" type="x-p"/> Like the noise of chariots - Bochart also remarks: - "The locusts fly with a great noise, so as to be heard six miles off, and while they are eating the fruits of the earth, the sound of them is like that of a flame driven by the wind." <div eID="gen34092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34093" type="x-p"/> Ibid., p. 478.
entries.057af51d3baf3f43d615b12c3d4f6f36c920a0f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34094" type="x-p"/> All faces shall gather blackness - Universal mourning shall take place, because they know that such a plague is irresistible.
entries.b3e58558eba046516a0e42c584de632c3f587863: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34095" type="x-p"/> Like mighty men - like men of war (and as horsemen, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.4">Joe 2:4</reference>) - The prophet does not say they are such, but they resemble. They are locusts; but in their operations they are Like the above. <div eID="gen34095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34096" type="x-p"/> They shall not break their ranks - See the account on <reference osisRef="Joe.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>, from Dr. Shaw.
entries.0263822f01b5dca4192e5b92d76b1ed6d9389b1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34097" type="x-p"/> They shall not be wounded - They have hard scales like a coat of mail; but the expression refers to the utter uselessness of all means to prevent their depredations. See Shaw's account above.
entries.1372aa59ad123961fafd1e22c5fecc113e7765df: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34098" type="x-p"/> The earth shall quake - the heavens shall tremble - Poetical expressions, to point out universal consternation and distress. The earth quaked to see itself deprived of its verdure; the heavens trembled to find themselves deprived of their light. <div eID="gen34098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34099" type="x-p"/> The sun and the moon shall be dark - Bochart relates that "their multitude is sometimes so immense as to obscure the heavens for the space of twelve miles!" - Ibid. p. 479.
entries.d6f90dc5892428e51d1f3a03374c71eaaf00b77a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34100" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall utter his voice - Such a mighty force seems as if summoned by the Almighty, and the noise they make in coming announces their approach, while yet afar off.
entries.32dfb844d62015a53935b6520e5d0e20aa45c0bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34101" type="x-p"/> Turn ye even to me - Three means of turning are recommended: Fasting, weeping, mourning, i.e., continued sorrow.
entries.f53720d84a6c725ba29f565c5b1c2eceef5f7b30: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34102" type="x-p"/> Rend your heart - Let it not be merely a rending of your garments, but let your hearts be truly contrite. Merely external worship and hypocritical pretensions will only increase the evil, and cause God to meet you with heavier judgments. <div eID="gen34102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34103" type="x-p"/> For he is gracious - Good and benevolent in his own nature. <div eID="gen34103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34104" type="x-p"/> Merciful - Pitying and forgiving, as the effect of goodness and benevolence. <div eID="gen34104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34105" type="x-p"/> Slow to anger - He is not easily provoked to punish, because he is gracious and merciful. <div eID="gen34105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34106" type="x-p"/> Of great kindness - Exuberant goodness to all them that return to him. <div eID="gen34106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34107" type="x-p"/> And repenteth him of the evil - Is ever ready to change his purpose to destroy, when he finds the culprit willing to be saved. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.7">Exo 34:7</reference>.
entries.09805dbac27fc63d18cc04ba1e1e71e9586992c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34108" type="x-p"/> Who knoweth if he will return - He may yet interpose and turn aside the calamity threatened, and so far preserve the land from these ravagers, that there will be food for men and cattle, and a sufficiency of offerings for the temple service. Therefore: -
entries.82b6e07b53cfa66b47ec1ae50243b7ab0296ffd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen34108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34109" type="x-p"/> Blow the trumpet - Let no time be lost, let the alarm be sounded.
entries.eb161a1c676c8d2ab3a8069f3899f6375a3fe09d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen34109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34110" type="x-p"/> Gather the children - Let all share in the humiliation, for all must feel the judgment, should it come. Let no state nor condition among the people be exempted. The elders, the young persons, the infants, the bridegroom, and the bride; let all leave their houses, and go to the temple of God.
entries.60e5986ab6820da2802d479ea963541d3734ce7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen34110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34111" type="x-p"/> Let the priests - weep between the porch and the altar - The altar of burnt-offerings stood before the porch of the temple, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12">2Chr 8:12</reference>, and between them there was an open space of fifteen or twenty cubits. It was there that the priests prostrated themselves on such occasions. It was into this place that the priests brought the sacrifice or victim of atonement; and where the high priest laid his hands on the head of the victim confessing his sins. <div eID="gen34111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34112" type="x-p"/> Let them say - The following was the form to be used on this occasion, "Spare thy people," etc. And if this be done with a rent heart, etc., "then will the Lord be jealous for his land, and pity his people," <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.18">2Chr 8:18</reference>. He will surely save, if ye seriously return to and penitently seek him.
entries.0f93698557aa89ee858ae3d4cda48148ab308970: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen34112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34113" type="x-p"/> Yea, the Lord will answer - It is not a peradventure; it will surely be done; if ye seek God as commanded, ye will find him as promised. <div eID="gen34113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34114" type="x-p"/> I will send you corn and wine - He will either prevent the total ravaging of the land, or so bless it with extraordinary vegetable strength, that ye shall have plentiful crops.
entries.a9aa2595207aa6be33270b0979dc0d7d3d14e00e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen34114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34115" type="x-p"/> I will remove far off from you the northern army - "That is, the locusts; which might enter Judea by the north, as Circassia and Mingrelia abound with them. Or the locusts may be thus called, because they spread terror like the Assyrian armies, which entered Judea by the north. See <reference osisRef="Zep.2.13">Zep 2:13</reference>." - Newcome. Syria, which was northward of Judea, was infested with them; and it must have been a northern wind that brought them into Judea, in the time of Joel; as God promises to change this wind, and carry them into a barren and desolate land, Arabia Deserta. "And his face toward the east sea," i.e., the Dead Sea, which lay eastward of Jerusalem. "His hinder part toward the utmost sea," the western sea, i.e., the Mediterranean. <div eID="gen34115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34116" type="x-p"/> And his stink shalt come up - After having been drowned by millions in the Mediterranean, the reflux of the tide has often brought them back, and thrown there in heaps upon the shore, where they putrefied in such a manner as to infect the air and produce pestilence, by which both men and cattle have died in great multitudes. See Bochart, Hieroz., vol. ii., p. 481. <div eID="gen34116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34117" type="x-p"/> Livy, and St. Augustine after him, relate that there was such an immense crowd of locusts in Africa that, having eaten up every green thing, a wind arose that carried them into the sea, where they perished; but being cast upon the shore, they putrefied, and bred such a pestilence, that eighty thousand men died of it in the kingdom of Massinissa, and thirty thousand in the garrison of Utica, in which only ten remained alive. See Calmet and Livy, lib. xc., and August. De Civitate Dei, lib. iv., c. 31. We have many testimonies of a similar kind. <div eID="gen34117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34118" type="x-p"/> Because he hath done great things - Or, כי ki, although he have done great things, or, after he has done them, i.e., in almost destroying the whole country.
entries.1c7f6b8d9e17f510af9c1a61ebd8718ff0908553: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen34118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34119" type="x-p"/> Fear not - for the Lord will do great things - The words are repeated from the preceding verse; Jehovah will do great things in driving them away, and supernaturally restoring the land to fertility.
entries.a88dfafb1aecfba935e9f7a49506f97766170396: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen34119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34120" type="x-p"/> The former rain moderately - המורה לצדקה hammoreh litsedakah, "the former rain in righteousness," that is, in due time and in just proportion. This rain fell after autumn, the other in spring. See <reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Hos 6:3</reference>. <div eID="gen34120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34121" type="x-p"/> In the first month - בראשון barishon, "as aforetime." So Bp. Newcome. In the month Nisan. - Syriac.
entries.8cd12877056680c744f37087e4649f88bb7b1cb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen34121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34122" type="x-p"/> I will restore - the years - It has already been remarked that the locusts not only destroyed the produce of that year, but so completely ate up all buds, and barked the trees, that they did not recover for some years. Here God promises that he would either prevent or remedy that evil; for he would restore the years that the locusts, cankerworm, caterpillar, and palmerworm had eaten.
entries.bbbb59059a94456491f1ef5d82acb2a345788c88: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen34122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34123" type="x-p"/> Praise the name of the Lord your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you - In so destroying this formidable enemy; and so miraculously restoring the land to fertility, after so great a devastation.
entries.a54d0fa9d9a884b677accad871ccea82d2a9b2e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen34123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34124" type="x-p"/> Shall come to pass afterward - אחרי כן acharey ken, "after this;" the same, says Kimchi, as in the latter days, which always refers to the days of the Messiah; and thus this prophecy is to be interpreted: and we have the testimony of St. Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.2.17">Act 2:17</reference>, that this prophecy relates to that mighty effusion of the Holy Spirit which took place after the day of pentecost. Nor is there any evidence that such an effusion took place, nor such effects were produced, from the days of this prophet till the day of pentecost. And the Spirit was poured out then upon all flesh, that is, on people of different countries, speaking the languages of almost all the people of the earth; which intimated that these were the first-fruits of the conversion of all the nations of the world. For there was scarcely a tongue in the universe that was not to be found among the Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamians, Jews, Cappadocians, people of Pontus, of Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya, Cyrene, Rome, Crete, and Arabia, who were residents at Jerusalem at that time; and on whom this mighty gift was poured out, each hearing and apprehending the truths of the Gospel, in his own language wherein he was born. Thus we have Divine authority for saying, that was the fulfillment of this prophecy by Joel. And the mighty and rapid spread of the Gospel of Christ in the present day, by means of the translation of the Scriptures into almost all the regular languages of the world, and the sending missionaries to all nations, who preach the Gospel in those tongues, are farther proofs that the great promise is in the fullest progress to be speedily fulfilled, even in the utmost sense of the words. <div eID="gen34124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34125" type="x-p"/> Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy - Shall preach - exhort, pray, and instruct, so as to benefit the Church. <div eID="gen34125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34126" type="x-p"/> Your old men shall dream dreams - Have my will represented to them in this way, as the others by direct inspiration. <div eID="gen34126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34127" type="x-p"/> Your young men shall see visions - Have true representations of Divine things made upon their imaginations by the power of God; that they shall have as full an evidence of them as they could have of any thing that came to the mind through the medium of the senses.
entries.c330c8f2b36a9412cc840dec91e745e7c8e8fbbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen34127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34128" type="x-p"/> And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids - The gifts of teaching and instructing men shall not be restricted to any one class or order of people. He shall call and qualify the men of his own choice; and shall take such out of all ranks, orders, degrees, and offices in society. And he will pour out his Spirit upon them; and they shall be endowed with all the gifts and graces necessary to convert sinners, and build up the Church of Christ on its most holy faith. <div eID="gen34128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34129" type="x-p"/> And this God has done, and is still doing. He left the line of Aaron, and took his apostles indiscriminately from any tribe. He passed by the regular order of the priesthood, and the public schools of the most celebrated doctors, and took his evangelists from among fishermen, tent-makers, and even the Roman tax-gatherers. And he, lastly, passed by the Jewish tribes, and took the Gentile converts, and made them preachers of righteousness to the inhabitants of the whole earth. The same practice he continues to the present day; yet he did not then pass by a man brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, no more than he would now a man brought up in a celebrated seminary of learning. He is ever free to use his own gifts, in his own way; and when learning is sanctified, by being devoted to the service of God, and the possessor is humble and pious, and has those natural gifts necessary for a public teacher, perhaps we might safely say, God would in many cases prefer such: but he will have others, as intimated in the prophecy, that we may see the conversion of men is not by human might, nor power, but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts. The learned man can do nothing without his Spirit; the unlearned must have his gifts and graces, without which both their labors would be unprofitable; and thus the excellency of the power is of God, and no flesh can glory in his presence. See my sermon on this passage.
entries.8de62f097a276d8ac350abeb294579bf874a14f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen34129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34130" type="x-p"/> Wonders in the heavens and in the earth - This refers to those dreadful sights, dreadful portents, and destructive commotion, by which the Jewish polity was finally overthrown, and the Christian religion established in the Roman empire. See how our Lord applies this prophecy, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.29">Mat 24:29</reference> (note), and the parallel texts.
entries.7cd1681a5513ef22b6d539c7ee139abc87908645: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen34130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34131" type="x-p"/> The sun shall be turned into darkness - The Jewish polity, civil and ecclesiastical, shall be entirely destroyed. <div eID="gen34131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34132" type="x-p"/> Before the great and the terrible day of the Lord come - In the taking and sacking of Jerusalem, and burning of the temple, by the Romans, under Titus, the son of Vespasian. This was, perhaps, the greatest and most terrible day of God's vengeance ever shown to the world, or that ever will be shown, till the great day of the general judgment. For a full view of this subject, I wish to refer the reader to the notes on Matthew 24.
entries.234908efe6867a5f06942d7ffa7d851bce07cafc: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen34132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34133" type="x-p"/> Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord - כל אשר יקרא בשם יהוה col asher yikra beshem Yehovah, "All who shall invoke in the name of Jehovah." That Christ is the Jehovah here mentioned appears plain from <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Rom 10:15</reference>, where the reader had better consult the notes. "This refers," says Bp. Newcome, "to the safety of the Christians during the Jewish and the Roman war." It may: but it has a much more extensive meaning, as the use of it by St. Paul, as above, evidently shows. Every man who invokes Jehovah for mercy and salvation by or in the name, Jesus - that very name given under heaven among men for this purpose - shall be saved. Nor is there salvation in any other; and those who reject him had better lay these things to heart before it be too late. <div eID="gen34133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34134" type="x-p"/> For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem - Our blessed Lord first began to preach the Gospel in Mount Zion, in the temple, and throughout Jerusalem. There he formed his Church, and thence he sent his apostles and evangelists to every part of the globe: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the Gospel to every creature." Of the Jews there was but a remnant, a very small number, that received the doctrine of the Gospel, here termed the remnant that the Lord should call; קרא kore, whom he calleth. Many were called who would not obey: but those who obeyed the call were saved; and still he delivers those who call upon him; and he is still calling on men to come to him that they may be saved.  <chapter eID="Joel.2"/> <div eID="gen34134" type="x-p"/>

entries.eafff39920b4eea2cd964aea745c77feae89211d: <div eID="gen16296" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Summons to Penitential Prayer for the Removal of the Judgment - <reference osisRef="Joel.2.1-Joel.2.17">Joel 2:1-17</reference></title> <div sID="gen16297" type="x-p"/> This section does not contain a fresh or second address of the prophet, but simply forms the second part of his sermon of repentance, in which he repeats with still greater emphasis the command already hinted at in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14-Joel.1.15">Joe 1:14-15</reference>, that there should be a meeting of the congregation for humiliation and prayer, and assigns the reason in a comprehensive picture of the approach of Jehovah’s great and terrible judgment-day (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.1-Joel.2.11">Joe 2:1-11</reference>), coupled with the cheering assurance that the Lord will still take compassion upon His people, according to His great grace, if they will return to Him with all their heart (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.12-Joel.2.14">Joe 2:12-14</reference>); and then closes with another summons to the whole congregation to assemble for this purpose in the house of the Lord, and with instructions how the priests are to pray to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.15-Joel.2.17">Joe 2:15-17</reference>). <div eID="gen16297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16298" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Joel.2.1">Joe 2:1</reference> <div eID="gen16298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16299" type="x-p"/> By blowing the far-sounding horn, the priests are to make known to the people the coming of the judgment, and to gather them together in the temple to pray. Joe 2:1. <hi type="italic">“Blow ye the trumpet upon Zion, and cause it to sound upon my holy mountain! All the inhabitants of the land shall tremble; for the day of Jehovah cometh, for it is near.” </hi> That this summons is addressed to the priests, is evident from <reference osisRef="Joel.2.15">Joe 2:15</reference>, compared with Joe 2:14. On <hi type="italic">tiq‛ū shōphâr</hi> and <hi type="italic">hârı̄‛ū</hi>, see at Hos 5:8. “Upon Zion,” i.e., from the top of the temple mountain. Zion is called the holy mountain, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>, because the Lord was there enthroned in His sanctuary, on the summit of Moriah, which He claimed as His own. <hi type="italic">Râgaz</hi>, to tremble, i.e., to start up from their careless state (Hitzig). On the expression, “for the day of Jehovah cometh,” see Joe 1:15. By the position of בּוא at the head of the sentence, and that in the perfect בּא instead of the imperfect, as in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.15">Joe 1:15</reference>, the coming of the day of Jehovah is represented as indisputably certain. The addition of <hi type="italic">kı̄ qârōbh</hi> (for it is near) cannot be accounted for, however, from the fact that in the spiritual intuition of the prophet this day had already come, whereas in reality it was only drawing near (Hengstenberg); for such a separation as this between one element of prophesying and another is inconceivable. The explanation is simply, that the day of the Lord runs throughout the history of the kingdom of God, so that it occurs in each particular judgment: not, however, as fully manifested, but simply as being near or approaching, so far as its complete fulfilment is concerned. Joel now proclaims the coming of the day in its full completion, on the basis of the judgment already experienced, as the approach of a terrible army of locusts that darkens the land, at the head of which Jehovah is riding in all the majesty of the Judge of the world. The description is divided into three strophes thus: he first of all depicts the sight of this army of God, as seen afar off, and its terrible appearance in general (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Joel.2.3">Joe 2:3</reference>); then the appearance and advance of this mighty army (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.4-Joel.2.6">Joe 2:4-6</reference>); and lastly, its irresistible power (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.7-Joel.2.11">Joe 2:7-11</reference>); and closes the first strophe with a figurative description of the devastation caused by this terrible army, whilst in the second and third he gives prominence to the terror which they cause among all nations, and over all the earth.
entries.949a2219f6371880178c84e860c1fba8f4184e89: <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2-Joel.2.3">Joe 2:2-3</reference> <hi type="italic">“A day of darkness and obscurity, a day of clouds and cloudy night: like morning dawn spread over the mountains, a people great and strong: there has not been the like from all eternity, nor will there be after it even to the years of generation and generation.</hi> Joe 2:3. <hi type="italic">Before it burneth fire, and behind it flameth flame: the land before it as the garden of Eden, and behind it like a desolate wilderness; and even that which escaped did not remain to it.” </hi> With four words, expressing the idea of darkness and obscurity, the day of Jehovah is described as a day of the manifestation of judgment. The words חשׁך ענן וערפל are applied in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.11">Deu 4:11</reference> to the cloudy darkness in which Mount Sinai was enveloped, when Jehovah came down upon it in the fire; and in <reference osisRef="Exod.10.22">Exo 10:22</reference>, the darkness which fell upon Egypt as the ninth plague is called אפלה. כּשׁחר וגו does not belong to what precedes, nor does it mean blackness or twilight (as Ewald and some Rabbins suppose), but “the morning dawn.” The subject to <hi type="italic">pârus</hi> (spread) is neither <hi type="italic">yōm</hi> (day), which precedes it, nor <hi type="italic">‛am</hi> (people), which follows; for neither of these yields a suitable thought at all. The subject is left indefinite: “like morning dawn is it spread over the mountains.” The prophet’s meaning is evident enough from what follows. He clearly refers to the bright glimmer or splendour which is seen in the sky as a swarm of locusts approaches, from the reflection of the sun’s rays from their wings.<note placement="foot">The following is the account given by the Portuguese monk Francis Alvarez, in his <hi type="italic">Journey through Abyssinia</hi> (Oedmann, <hi type="italic">Vermischte Sammlungen</hi>, vi. p. 75): “The day before the arrival of the locusts we could infer that they were coming, from a yellow reflection in the sky, proceeding from their yellow wings. As soon as this light appeared, no one had the slightest doubt that an enormous swarm of locusts was approaching.” He also says, that during his stay in the town of Barua he himself saw this phenomenon, and that so vividly, that even the earth had a yellow colour from the reflection. The next day a swarm of locusts came.</note> <div eID="gen16299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16300" type="x-p"/> With עם רב ועצוּם (a people great and strong) we must consider the verb בּא (cometh) in <reference osisRef="Exod.10.1">Exo 10:1</reference> as still retaining its force. <hi type="italic">Yōm</hi> (day) and <hi type="italic">‛âm</hi> (people) have the same predicate, because the army of locusts carries away the day, and makes it into a day of cloudy darkness. The darkening of the earth is mentioned in connection with the Egyptian plague of locusts in <reference osisRef="Exod.10.15">Exo 10:15</reference>, and is confirmed by many witnesses (see the comm. on Ex. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>). The fire and the flame which go both before and behind the great and strong people, viz., the locusts, cannot be understood as referring to the brilliant light kindled as it were by the morning dawn, which proceeds from the fiery armies of the vengeance of God, i.e., the locusts (Umbreit), nor merely to the burning heat of the drought by which everything is consumed (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.19">Joe 1:19</reference>); but this burning heat is heightened here into devouring flames of fire, which accompany the appearing of God as He comes to judgment at the head of His army, after the analogy of the fiery phenomena connected with the previous manifestations of God, both in Egypt, where a terrible hail fell upon the land before the plague of locusts, accompanied by thunder and balls of fire (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.23-Exod.9.24">Exo 9:23-24</reference>), and also at Sinai, upon which the Lord came down amidst thunder and lightning, and spoke to the people out of the fire (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.16-Exod.19.18">Exo 19:16-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.11-Deut.4.12">Deu 4:11-12</reference>). The land, which had previously resembled the garden of paradise (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.8">Gen 2:8</reference>), was changed in consequence into a desolate wilderness. פּליטה does not mean escape or deliverance, either here or in Oba 1:17, but simply that which has run away or escaped. Here it signifies that part of the land which has escaped the devastation; for it is quite contrary to the usage of the language to refer לו, as most commentators do, to the swarm of locusts, from which there is no escape, no deliverance (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.14">2Sa 15:14</reference>; Jdg 21:17; Ezr 9:13, in all of which ל refers to the subject, to which the thing that escaped was assigned). Consequently לו can only refer to הארץ. The perfect היתה stands related to אחריו, according to which the swarm of locusts had already completed the devastation.
entries.322db2febab43162a359ef4731a6f7f91b8ce8a0: <reference osisRef="Joel.2.4-Joel.2.6">Joe 2:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen16300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16301" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Joel.2.4-Joel.2.6">Joe 2:4-6</reference> we have a description of this mighty army of God, and of the alarm caused by its appearance among all nations. Joe 2:4. <hi type="italic">“Like the appearance of horses is its appearance; and like riding-horses, so do they run.</hi> Joe 2:5. <hi type="italic">Like rumbling of chariots on the tops of the mountains do they leap, like the crackling of flame which devours stubble, like a strong people equipped for conflict.</hi> Joe 2:6. <hi type="italic">Before it nations tremble; all faces withdraw their redness.” </hi> The comparison drawn between the appearance of the locusts and that of horses refers chiefly to the head, which, when closely examined, bears a strong resemblance to the head of a horse, as Theodoret has already observed; a fact which gave rise to their being called <hi type="italic">Heupferde</hi> (hay-horses) in German. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Joel.2.4">Joe 2:4</reference></hi> the rapidity of their motion is compared to the running of riding-horses (<hi type="italic">pârâshı̄m</hi>); and in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.5">Joe 2:5</reference> the noise caused by their springing motion to the rattling of chariots, the small two-wheeled war-chariots of the ancients, when driven rapidly over the rough mountain roads. The noise caused by their devouring the plants and shrubs is also compared to the burning of a flame over a stubble-field that has been set on fire, and their approach to the advance of a war force equipped for conflict. (Compare the adoption and further expansion of these similes in <reference osisRef="Rev.9.7">Rev 9:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.9">Rev 9:9</reference>). At the sight of this terrible army of God the nations tremble, so that their faces grow pale. <hi type="italic">‛Ammı̄m</hi> means neither people (see at 1Ki 22:28) nor the tribes of Israel, but nations generally. Joel is no doubt depicting something more here than the devastation caused by the locusts in his own day. There are differences of opinion as to the rendering of the second hemistich, which Nahum repeats in Joe 2:11. The combination of פּארוּר with פּרוּר, a pot (Chald., Syr., Jer., Luth., and others), is untenable, since פּרוּר comes from פּרר, to break in pieces, whereas פּארוּר (= פּארוּר) is from the root פאר, <hi type="italic">piel</hi>, to adorn, beautify, or glorify; so that the rendering, “they gather redness,” i.e., glow with fear, which has an actual but not a grammatical support in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.8">Isa 13:8</reference>, is evidently worthless. We therefore understand פּארוּר, as Ab. Esr., Abul Wal., and others have done, in the sense of <hi type="italic">elegantia, nitor, pulchritudo,</hi> and as referring to the splendour or healthy ruddiness of the cheeks, and take קבּץ ekat dn as an intensive form of קבץ, in the sense of drawing into one’s self, or withdrawing, inasmuch as fear and anguish cause the blood to fly from the face and extremities to the inward parts of the body. For the fact of the face turning pale with terror, see Jer 30:6.
entries.51d58099d9f3634d5852af0b5c91efa1d4fb15ef: <reference osisRef="Joel.2.7-Joel.2.9">Joe 2:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen16301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16302" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Joel.2.7-Joel.2.10">Joe 2:7-10</reference> the comparison of the army of locusts to a well-equipped army is carried out still further; and, in the first place, by a description of the irresistible force of its advance. Joe 2:7. <hi type="italic">“They run like heroes, like warriors they climb the wall; every one goes on its way, and they do not change their paths.</hi> Joe 2:8. <hi type="italic">And they do not press one another, they go every one in his path; and they fall headlong through weapons, and do not cut themselves in pieces.</hi> Joe 2:9. <hi type="italic">They run about in the city, they run upon the wall, they climb into the houses, they come through the windows like a thief.” </hi> This description applies for the most part word for word to the advance of the locusts, as Jerome (in loc.) and Theodoret (on <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Joel.2.8">Joe 2:8</reference></hi>) attest from their own observation.<note placement="foot">Jerome says: “We saw (<hi type="italic">al.</hi> heard) this lately in the province (Palestine). For when the swarms of locusts come and fill the whole atmosphere between the earth and sky, they fly in such order, according to the appointment of the commanding God, that they preserve an exact shape, just like the squares drawn upon a tesselated pavement, not diverging on either side by, so to speak, so much as a finger’s breadth. <hi type="italic">'And,'</hi> as he (the prophet) interprets the metaphor, <hi type="italic">'through the windows they will fall, and not be destroyed.'</hi> For there is no road impassable to locusts; they penetrate into fields, and crops, and trees, and cities, and houses, and even the recesses of the bed-chambers.” And Theodoret observes on <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Joel.2.8">Joe 2:8</reference></hi>: “For you may see the grasshopper like a hostile army ascending the walls, and advancing along the roads, and not suffering any difficulty to disperse them, but steadily moving forward, as if according to some concerted plan.” And again, on <reference osisRef="Joel.2.9">Joe 2:9</reference> : “And this we have frequently seen done, not merely by hostile armies, but also by locusts, which not only when flying, but by creeping along the walls, pass through the windows into the houses themselves.”</note> <div eID="gen16302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16303" type="x-p"/> They run like heroes - namely, to the assault: רוּץ referring to an attack, as in <reference osisRef="Job.15.26">Job 15:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.18.30">Psa 18:30</reference>, “as their nimbleness has already been noticed in Joe 2:4” (Hitzig). Their climbing the walls also points to an assault. Their irresistible march to the object of their attack is the next point described. No one comes in another’s way; they do not twist (עבט) their path, i.e., do not diverge either to the right hand or to the left, so as to hinder one another. Even the force of arms cannot stop their advance. שׁלח is not a missile, <hi type="italic">telum</hi>, <hi type="italic">missile</hi> (Ges. and others), but a weapon extended or held in front (Hitzig); and the word is not only applied to a sword (<reference osisRef="2Chr.23.10">2Ch 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.4.11">Neh 4:11</reference>), but to weapons of defence (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:5</reference>). בּצע, not “to wound themselves” (= פּצע), but “to cut in pieces,” used here intransitively, to cut themselves in pieces. This does no doubt transcend the nature even of the locust; but it may be explained on the ground that they are represented as an invincible army of God.<note placement="foot">The notion that these words refer to attempts to drive away the locusts by force of arms, in support of which Hitzig appeals to <hi type="italic">Liv. hist.</hi> xlii. 10, <hi type="italic">Plinii hist. n.</hi> xi. 29, and Hasselquist, <hi type="italic">Reise nach Pal.</hi> p. 225, is altogether inappropriate. All that Livy does is to speak of <hi type="italic">ingenti agmine hominum ad colligendas eas (locustas) coacto</hi>; and Pliny merely says, <hi type="italic">Necare et in Syria militari imperio coguntur.</hi> And although Hasselquist says, Both in Asia and Europe they sometimes take the field against the locusts with all the equipments of war,” this statement is decidedly false so far as Europe is concerned. In Bessarabia (according to the accounts of eye-witnesses) they are merely in the habit of scaring away the swarms of locusts that come in clouds, by making a great noise with drums, kettles, hay-forks, and other noisy instruments, for the purpose of preventing them from settling on the ground, and so driving them further. Hass’s account of a pasha of Tripoli having sent 4000 soldiers against the insects only a few years ago, is far too indefinite to prove that they were driven away by the force of arms.</note> <div eID="gen16303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16304" type="x-p"/> On the other hand, the words of <reference osisRef="Joel.2.9">Joe 2:9</reference> apply, so far as the first half is concerned, both to the locusts and to an army (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.33.4">Isa 33:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.5">Nah 2:5</reference>); whereas the second half applies only to the former, of which Theodoret relates in the passage quoted just now, that he has frequently seen this occur (compare also <reference osisRef="Exod.10.6">Exo 10:6</reference>).
entries.ce7f4bace22316b0b2235584afb8ccf3b12e98d9: <reference osisRef="Joel.2.10-Joel.2.11">Joe 2:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen16304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16305" type="x-p"/> The whole universe trembles at this judgment of God. Joe 2:10. <hi type="italic">“Before it the earth quakes, the heavens tremble: sun and moon have turned black, and the stars have withdrawn their shining.</hi> Joe 2:11. <hi type="italic">And Jehovah thunders before His army, for His camp is very great, for the executor of His word is strong; for the day of Jehovah is great and very terrible, and who can endure it?” </hi> The remark of Jerome on <reference osisRef="Joel.2.10">Joe 2:10</reference>, viz., that “it is not that the strength of the locusts is so great that they can move the heavens and shake the earth, but that to those who suffer from such calamities, from the amount of their own terror, the heavens appear to shake and the earth to reel,” is correct enough so far as the first part is concerned, but it by no means exhausts the force of the words. For, as Hitzig properly observes, the earth could only quake because of the locusts when they had settled, and the heavens could only tremble and be darkened when they were flying, so that the words would in any case be very much exaggerated. But it by no means follows from this, that לפניו is not to be taken as referring to the locusts, like מפּניו in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.6">Joe 2:6</reference>, but to the coming of Jehovah in a storm, and that it is to be understood in this sense: “the earth quakes, the air roars at the voice of Jehovah, i.e., at the thunder, and storm-clouds darken the day.” For although <hi type="italic">nâthan qōlō</hi> (shall utter His voice) in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.11">Joe 2:11</reference> is to be understood as referring to the thunder, Joel is not merely describing a storm, which came when the trouble had reached its height and put an end to the plague of locusts (Credner, Hitzig, and others). לפניו cannot be taken in any other sense than that in which it occurs in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.3">Joe 2:3</reference>; that is to say, it can only refer to “the great people and strong,” viz., the army of locusts, like מפּניו. Heaven and earth tremble at the army of locusts, because Jehovah comes with them to judge the world (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.13">Isa 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.5-Nah.1.6">Nah 1:5-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10">Jer 10:10</reference>). The sun and moon become black, i.e., dark, and the stars withdraw their brightness (<hi type="italic">'âsaph</hi>, withdraw, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.19">1Sa 14:19</reference>), i.e., they let their light shine no more. That these words affirm something infinitely greater than the darkening of the lights of heaven by storm-clouds, is evident partly from the predictions of the judgment of the wrath of the Lord that is coming upon the whole earth and upon the imperial power (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Isa 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.7">Eze 32:7</reference>), at which the whole fabric of the universe trembles and nature clothes itself in mourning, and partly from the adoption of this particular feature by Christ in His description of the last judgment (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Mat 24:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.13.24-Mark.13.25">Mar 13:24-25</reference>). Compare, on the other hand, the poetical description of a storm in Psa 18:8., where this feature is wanting. (For further remarks, see at Joe 3:4.) At the head of the army which is to execute His will, the Lord causes His voice of thunder to sound (<hi type="italic">nâthan qōl</hi>, to thunder; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.14">Psa 18:14</reference>, etc.). The reason for this is given in three sentences that are introduced by <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi>. Jehovah does this because His army is very great; because this powerful army executes His word, i.e., His command; and because the day of judgment is so great and terrible, that no one can endure it, i.e., no one can stand before the fury of the wrath of the Judge (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10">Jer 10:10</reference>; Mal 3:1).
entries.4eb6796e986f89866c0f5bcedc97831b09922ca8: <reference osisRef="Joel.2.12-Joel.2.14">Joe 2:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen16305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16306" type="x-p"/> But there is still time to avert the completion of the judgment by sincere repentance and mourning; for God is merciful, and ready to forgive the penitent. Joe 2:12. <hi type="italic">“Yet even now, is the saying of Jehovah, turn ye to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.</hi> Joe 2:13. <hi type="italic">And rend your heart and not your garments, and turn back to Jehovah your God; for He is gracious and merciful, long-suffering, and great in kindness, and suffers Himself to repent of the evil.</hi> Joe 2:14. <hi type="italic">Who knoweth He turns and repents, and leaves behind Him blessing, meat-offering and drink-offering for Jehovah your God?” </hi> As the plague of locusts was intended to bring the people to reflect upon their conduct towards the Lord, so was the announcement of the great day of judgment and all its terrors made with no other object than to produce repentance and conversion, and thereby promote the good of the people of God. Joel therefore appends to the threatening of judgment a summons to sincere conversion to the Lord; and this he does by first of all addressing the summons to the people as a saying of Jehovah (v. 12), and then explaining this word of God in the most emphatic manner (vv. 13, 14). The Lord God requires conversion to Himself with all the heart (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3">1Sa 7:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.6.5">Deu 6:5</reference>; and for שׂוּב עד, Hos 14:2), associated with deep-rooted penitence on account of sin, which is to be outwardly manifested in fasting and mourning. But lest the people should content themselves with the outward signs of mourning, he proceeds in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joe 2:13</reference> with the warning admonition, “Rend your heart, and not your garments.” Rending the heart signifies contrition of heart (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.19">Psa 51:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.26">Eze 36:26</reference>). He then assigns the motive for this demand, by pointing to the mercy and grace of God, in the words of <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>, with which the Lord made known to Moses His inmost nature, except that in the place of ואמת, which we find in this passage, he adds, on the ground of the facts recorded in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.14">Eze 32:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.16">2Sa 24:16</reference>, ונחם על הרעה. On the strength of these facts he hopes, even in the present instance, for forgiveness on the part of God, and the removal of the judgment. “Who knoweth?” equivalent to “perhaps;” not because “too confident a hope would have had in it something offensive to Jehovah” (Hitzig), but “lest perchance they might either despair on account of the magnitude of their crimes, or the greatness of the divine clemency might make them careless” (Jerome).<note placement="foot">“He speaks after the manner of a terrified conscience, which is lifted up again with difficulty after a season of affliction, and begins to aspire after hope and the mercy of God. Moreover, the expression 'who knoweth' is a Hebrew phrase, which does not indicate doubt, but rather affirmation, coupled with desire, as if we were to say, 'And yet surely God will turn again.'” - Luther, <hi type="italic">Enarrat. in Joelem, Opp.,</hi> Jena 1703, p. iii.</note> ישׁוּב, to turn, sc. from coming to judgment. נהם as in Joe 2:13. השׁאיר אחריו, to leave behind Him, sc. when He returns to His throne in heaven (Hos 5:15). <hi type="italic">Berâkhâh</hi>, a blessing, viz., harvest-produce for a meat-offering and drink-offering, which had been destroyed by the locusts (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.9">Joe 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.13">Joe 1:13</reference>).
entries.95327d70b2a74ef44f6ea91e3d957c00e7b716d2: <reference osisRef="Joel.2.15-Joel.2.17">Joe 2:15-17</reference> <div eID="gen16306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16307" type="x-p"/> To make this admonition still more emphatic, the prophet concludes by repeating the appeal for the appointment of a meeting in the temple for prayer, and even gives the litany in which the priests are to offer their supplication. Joe 2:15. <hi type="italic">“Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, proclaim a meeting.</hi> Joe 2:16. <hi type="italic">Gather the people together, sanctify an assembly, bring together the old men, gather together the children and sucklings at the breasts. Let the bridegroom go out of his chamber, and the bride out of her room.</hi> Joe 2:17. <hi type="italic">Between the porch and the altar are the priests, the servants of Jehovah, to weep and say, Spare, O Jehovah, Thy people, and give not up Thine inheritance to shame, so that the heathen scoff at them. Wherefore should men say among the nations, Where is their God?” </hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.2.15">Joe 2:15</reference> is a literal repetition from <reference osisRef="Joel.2.1">Joe 2:1</reference> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference></hi>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.16">Joe 1:16</reference> a more detailed expansion of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference></hi>, in which, first of all, the people generally (עם) are mentioned, and then the objection of the summons explained in the words קדּשׁוּ קהל, “Call a holy meeting of the congregation.” But in order that none may think themselves exempt, the people are more precisely defined as old men, children, and sucklings. Even the bride and bridegroom are to give up the delight of their hearts, and take part in the penitential and mournful worship. No age, no rank, is to stay away, because no one, not even the suckling, is free from sin; but all, without exception, are exposed to the judgment. “A stronger proof of the deep and universal guilt of the whole nation could not be found, than that on the great day of penitence and prayer, even new-born infants were to be carried in their arms” (Umbreit). The penitential supplication of the whole nation is to be brought before the Lord by the priests as the mediators of the nation. יבכּוּ in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.17">Joe 1:17</reference> is jussive, like יצא in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.16">Joe 1:16</reference>, though Hitzig disputes this, but on insufficient grounds. The allusion to the priests in the former could only be unsuitable, if they were merely commanded to go to the temple like the rest of the people. But it is not to this that <reference osisRef="Joel.1.17">Joe 1:17</reference> refers, but to the performance of their official duty, when the people had assembled for the penitential festival. They were to stand between the porch of the temple and the altar of burnt-offering, i.e., immediately in front of the door of the holy place, and there with tears entreat the Lord, who was enthroned in the sanctuary, not to give up the people of His possession (<hi type="italic">nachălâh</hi> as in 1Ki 8:51; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">Deu 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">Deu 32:9</reference>) to the reproach of being scoffed at by the heathen. למשׁל־בּם גּוים is rendered by Luther and others, “that heathen rule over them,” after the ancient versions; and <reference osisRef="Ps.106.41">Psa 106:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.15.6">Deu 15:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lam.5.8">Lam 5:8</reference>, might be appealed to in support of this rendering. But although grammatically allowable, it is not required by the parallelism, as Hengstenberg maintains.
